items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Earl Warren, Buddy Tate and myself, we’re the only ones left of the Basie band.

ctx.x: It was just stock arrangements. We had two trumpets and a trombone and the other trumpet player, he used to play all the solos, play all the firsts and I was just sitting there. So, one night, we were playing at this Masonic Hall on Long Street and when his time came to play he was having a drink at the bar, so I took his solo. From then on, gee whiz, every time he’d get ready to take a solo, I’d say, “I got it.” That was my first solo on Limehouse Blues, I never will forget it. Gee whiz, that was a thrill to…

think very few people know this except the older guys, Earl Warren, Buddy Tate and myself, we’re the only ones left of the Basie band. They remember, but John Hammond, he was responsible for the Count Basie band, period, because he brought Basie to New York. They had, you remember, the Camel Hour, and all the bands used to do it. The [radio] broadcast, that was a good gig you could do it for a month at a time, two months. Benny Goodman used to do it for the whole summer. John Hammond, he talked the President of…

items.title: 56706_Buddy Tate oral history interview
items.q: He come up and he dug Prez, me, Jo and Sweets and all night long, he sat there. We was playing a place called the Plantation

ctx.x: Zoot suit, yeah, the zoot suit. He had a hat that wide. So he came on, you know, we just thought he was one of the boys, one of the hip boys. He come up and he dug Prez, me, Jo and Sweets and all night long, he sat there. We was playing a place called the Plantation, Joe Watts' Plantation out in Watts. And -- Joe Morris' Plantation, rather, out in Watts. So all night long, he sat there with us and whenever we'd take a break, we'd

go to his table. He bought Prez -- Prez was drinking heavy. Jo was drinking his Hennesey, Sweets was drinking. Do you know, at the end of the night, he pulled his coat back like this, told Prez and Jo Jones where to be at 9:00 that next morning, says, "FBI." They knew where they lived and they says, "If you aren't there, we will come after you." And Prez -- it really got to Prez, you know. He -- you know, he was kind of sensitive and man, that high voice really came out. "Man, ain't that a bitch." Now, you can…

items.title: Buddy Tate interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995
items.q: And maybe four or five trombones. There’s Sweets and Buck. Vic Dickenson, Dan Minor.

ctx.x: What size was the band at that time? Who was —

Well, we got about one, two, three, got five saxes. One, two three. Let’s see Prez, Jack, yeah, there’s five saxes. One, two, three, four, five. Five saxophones. And maybe four or five trombones. There’s Sweets and Buck. Vic Dickenson, Dan Minor.
It seems to me that the players at that time were not only good players, but real personalities.
